## The bag's second half

[Section 1](01-trade-history.qmd) explained why a cheap supermarket bag *exists* after silver, war, and plant transfer. This lesson asks what an **estate** does once Chinese monopoly leaf is no longer the only farm.

Hold two pictures. In one, Fortune's packing cases and Assam identification finish the road *to* the monopoly break. In the other, cleared forest, migrant labor schedules, and a late-nineteenth-century British cupboard that no longer depends on Canton chests. Chemistry still lives in [Chapter 1](../module-01/index.qmd). Aisle words still live in [Tea basics](../../tea-basics.qmd). This sitting owns the **aftershock**—land, labor, and the commodity form that makes the bag cheap.

## From plant transfer to industrial crop

Botany and politics opened the door. Estates walked through it.

Assam tea was identified and validated decades before Fortune's China missions; Fortune layered Chinese *sinensis* cultivars, makers, and know-how onto an industry already underway—that hinge lives in Section 1.[^1][^2] What followed was not a few experimental plots. It was a landscape of plantations: frontier clearance, imported and managed labor, and commodity schedules that could feed a mass market.[^3]

Sharma's *Empire's Garden* is the scholarly spine for Assam: how the British remade a jungle-laden frontier into cultivated estates, then imported indentured labor when they claimed local peasants would not suit the work, and how more than a million migrants later reshaped the region's social landscape.[^3] That is history of land and people—not a spreadsheet of colonial profit shares invented on this page.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Assam / Darjeeling estate sketch (named trails only)"}
| Place / trail | What the sources support | Fence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Assam** | Engineered plantation landscape; indentured / migrant labor; racialized "coolie" construction; frontier clearance (Sharma)[^3] | Do not invent acreage or wage series here |
| **Darjeeling** | Named with Assam in Section 1's four-era hinge as late-19th-c. Raj gardens; detail stays thin unless a dedicated monograph is added later | Pointer, not a second Assam chapter |
| **Kew public history** | By **1890**, India supplied about **90%** of Britain's domestic tea market; blunt note on forest clearance and labor cost; Maniram Datta Barua executed after 1857[^1] | Kew narrative claim—not a new audit of company books |

Botanical networks that moved crops (Kew / colonial gardens) mostly stay with Section 1's plant-transfer beat; one bridge sentence is enough: botany enabled estates, estates remade society.[^2]
:::

## Land, labor, and the cheap cup

Open story stays human-scale. Clearing land for estates cost forests and lives—Kew's public history is blunt about coolies and elephants in the clearance story, and about Maniram, who had first told Robert Bruce about Assam leaf, being hanged after the 1857 uprising.[^1] Sharma follows how migrant settlement irrevocably changed Assam's social landscape and how racialized constructions of the tea laborer shaped later politics.[^3]

None of that licenses a slogan like "tea alone caused empire" or a homemade re-estimate of who kept plantation profits. Kew's page also says India was "only allowed to keep 15 percent of plantation profits"—we treat that as **Kew's narrative phrasing**, not an independently re-audited ledger on this site.[^1] Prefer Sharma for labor depth; keep Kew for the readable market-and-cost trail.

Your grocery bag is cheap partly because someone else's garden became an estate. That sentence is history. It is not a morality play with invented villains, and it is not Chapter 1's Assam-versus-*sinensis* tasting lesson.

::: {.callout-caution title="Honesty fence"}
- Refuse re-estimating colonial profit shares from this page.
- Refuse "tea alone caused…" claims already fenced in Section 1.
- Kew's ~1890 / ~90% Britain-market line and human-cost notes are **context for the cheap bag**, not a new econometric model.[^1]
- Chemistry of the cup still lives in Chapter 1; shopping labels live in Tea basics.
:::

## Optional foldout: Ceylon's coffee-to-tea switch

Assam is the spine. Ceylon (today's Sri Lanka) is the named second garden when you want another empire aftershock—coffee rust collapsing "King Coffee," then tea rising on estates such as Loolecondera under planter James Taylor.[^4]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Ceylon — Taylor, Loolecondera, coffee rust → tea"}
McCarthy and Devine's *Tea and Empire* reconstructs Taylor's Victorian planter life and the coffee→tea transition, using his letters and plantation evidence—including the dark side of planting life, not only celebration.[^4] Popular Ceylon-tea histories place early Loolecondera tea clearings in the late 1860s as coffee failed; treat those as companion color to the scholarly portrait, not as a second primary ledger on this page.[^4]

**Why it belongs here:** another estate form after monopoly China leaf—commodity rescue through replanting, with labor and land costs attached.  
**Why it stays a foldout:** Assam (Sharma + Kew) already carries the open-story aftershock; Ceylon deepens without stealing the plot.
:::

Chemistry still explains what is in the cup ([Chapter 1 · Plants](../module-01/01-plants.qmd)). Processing factories explain how leaf becomes grade ([Chapter 1 · Processing](../module-01/02-processing.qmd)). Tea basics still owns aisle words for strong black and bag. The next history section asks how *people script* the drink regionally—Chaoshan tables, Taiwan tea art, Hong Kong milk-tea counters—not how empires priced the leaf.
